discovery: Quantum key distribution: physics-based secure communication (BB84 and entanglement-based E91 protocols)

nominees.name: Charles H. Bennett
nominees.affiliation: IBM Thomas J. Watson Research Center, USA

nominees.name: Artur Ekert
nominees.affiliation: University of Oxford, UK, and Centre for Quantum Technologies, National University of Singapore

motivation: Bennett and Brassard (BB84, 1984) showed that the laws of quantum physics (the no-cloning theorem and the disturbance caused by measurement) can guarantee the secrecy of a shared key, so security no longer depends on assumptions about how hard a computation is. With their 1992 experiment, they turned quantum measurement into a working communication primitive. Ekert (E91, 1991) independently linked key secrecy to the violation of Bell inequalities. This made nonlocality, a foundational question, into a working security resource and laid the conceptual basis for device-independent cryptography and certified randomness. Together, these ideas created the field of quantum communication. QKD now runs over metropolitan fibre networks, in daylight free-space links and between satellites and ground stations, and it underpins the emerging quantum internet. Few conceptual advances in physics have moved so directly from fundamental principles to deployed infrastructure.
